alalal-e91045-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 1: whether faith can grow.

alalal-e91045-d1e113.summary: First argument from Hugh of Saint Victor's De sacramentis: faith grows in two respects, cognition, when instructed toward knowledge, and affection, when stirred to devotion and strengthened in constancy.

alalal-e91045-d1e143.summary: Second argument, against restricting growth to illumination: Hugh says faith grew over time in all, not changing but increasing; before the law God was believed as creator and salvation awaited, but by whom and how it would be accomplished was unknown to most except a few; so articles about Christ's humanity were not then held, and faith grew in the number of articles. Also, God told Moses he had not revealed the name Adonai to the patriarchs but later did.

alalal-e91045-d1e201.summary: Fourth argument: Psalm 118:100, 'I understood more than the elders', suggests the elders believed fewer articles.

alalal-e91045-d1e212.summary: Further: Acts 2:17 says the young will see visions and the old dream dreams, so the young see something of the credibles that the elders did not.

alalal-e91045-d1e230.summary: Further: Gregory says the knowledge of the spiritual Fathers grew with time, and the nearer to the Saviour's coming, the more fully they grasped the mystery of salvation.

alalal-e91045-d1e254.summary: Fifth argument: in the creeds twelve articles became fourteen, and for the same cause they could be further distinguished, so faith grew and can grow in number of articles.

alalal-e91045-d1e272.summary: Sed contra: faith is a simple light illuminating toward eternal truth, which cannot grow, so neither can faith.

alalal-e91045-d1e283.summary: Second sed contra: in every article divine truth is presupposed and explained by what pertains to our salvation or what is eternally in God; the eternal cannot grow, and the temporal is an eternally ordained disposition that cannot increase.

alalal-e91045-d1e306.summary: Third sed contra: if the number of articles grew, faith would change in substance, since articles are its substance, which Lombard's text denies.

alalal-e91045-d1e324.summary: Fourth sed contra: implicit faith covers as many articles as explicit, since implicitness is on our side, not the articles'; the ancients' faith and ours differ only as implicit and explicit.

alalal-e91045-d1e342.summary: Fifth sed contra: if faith grew by explication, it would grow continually through the doctors' study, which no one says.

alalal-e91045-d1e358.summary: Solution, with Hugh: faith grows on the side of the believer, in intellect and affect, but not in itself or in what is believed. In intellect it grows in four ways: by revelation from above; by teaching that explains, as the Nicene Fathers expressed more about eternal generation and the Spirit's procession so that believers guarded against heresy; by the believed event coming to pass, since what is seen is better understood than what is foretold (Jerome); and by study, as faith seeks understanding (Anselm). In affect it grows in three ways: purifying affection from sin, removing the phantasms of natural reasons through devotion, and giving constancy, as in martyrdom. The articles themselves have not grown, since they rest on first truth, which alone fixes their number.
claims: Faith grows in the believer's understanding and affection, not in its articles.
The number of articles is fixed by first truth, not by human beings.

alalal-e91045-d1e474.summary: Reply to the first: Hugh means progress of the believer in faith rather than of faith in the believer.

alalal-e91045-d1e485.summary: Reply to the second: the articles did not grow in themselves, but their explanation and revelation did, which is growth only accidentally; though the passion may not have been known determinately to some, it was an article and was believed implicitly whenever any future deliverance was believed.
claims: Articles about Christ were believed implicitly in belief in future deliverance.

alalal-e91045-d1e508.summary: Reply to the Adonai text: it concerns not the manifestation of an article but of God himself, in which man grows day by day and never reaches perfectly, as Psalm 104:4 says, 'seek his face always'.

alalal-e91045-d1e530.summary: Reply to the three following authorities: they prove only human progress in knowing the articles, not growth in their number.

alalal-e91045-d1e541.summary: Reply to the last: articles are divided in many ways, but the reality remains one, considered differently, not increased, as conception and birth remain one reality whether counted as one or two.

alalal-e91045.summary: Article 1 of Distinction 25 asks whether faith can grow. Arguments from Hugh, Exodus 6:3, the Psalms, Joel and Gregory suggest that it grew historically even in the number of articles, and the creeds' expansion from twelve to fourteen articles seems to confirm this. Against this, faith's object is eternal truth and its articles are its substance. Albert holds, with Hugh, that faith grows on the side of the believer but not in itself or its articles. In understanding it grows by revelation, teaching, the fulfilment of events, and study; in affection by purification, freedom from rationalising phantasms, and constancy unto martyrdom. The number of articles is fixed by first truth. What grew historically was their explanation and revelation, the ancients believing implicitly what was later explicit. Different ways of counting the articles divide one reality without increasing it.
claims: Faith grows in the believer's understanding and affection, not in itself or in the number of its articles.
The articles rest on first truth, which alone fixes their number.
The ancients believed implicitly what was later made explicit.
